title: Indigenous-led photography project to reinterpret the wendigo
excerpt: Jamie Wetrade-Stevenson and Karen Murray are teaming up to create The Wendigo Project – photos, storytelling and a documentary about consuming modern culture.
content:
The creative directors of a new photography and storytelling project say Dene and Cree teachings about the wendigo have never been more relevant.

The creative duo behind The Wendigo Project is Yellowknife-based Tłıchǫ photographer and artist Jamie Wetrade-Stevenson and Karen Murray, a Dënesųłiné and Cree artist, designer and cultural worker based in Edmonton.

In Dene and Cree traditions, the wendigo – also known as the wheetago, among other names – is a malevolent and cannibalistic figure that features in cautionary stories about human greed, selfishness, imbalance and disconnection.

Instead of consuming people, Murray and Wetrade-Stevenson said their project will depict the wendigo consuming modern culture itself, including overconsumption, fast fashion, hoarded wealth and disposable technology.

Murray said she was inspired a year ago while going through “a little bit of emotional turmoil” and was reminded of a story about the wendigo she was told growing up.

“I was noticing similarities between my emotional turmoils, what’s going on socially in the world with the various political wars we have going on, the global animosities we have going on via conflicting social and religious views or realities,” she said.

“I felt like it’s a really great time right now, specifically with what’s going on, to be able to use my knowledge, my voice and tell the story – and not only that, but bring other community members in on it.”

Photography, storytelling and a documentary

The Wendigo Project will consist of a professional photography series, a short documentary by Tłı̨chǫ Dene filmmaker Sadetɫo Scott capturing the creative process, and a digital bundle featuring storytelling and conversations about what these teachings mean today.

Indigenous storytellers set to be featured in the project so far include Dehcho Dene broadcaster Lawrence Nayally, Tłı̨chǫ storytellers Janelle Nitsiza and Therese Zoe, and Cree Elder Rose Wabasca.

Wetrade-Stevenson said it was important that the project was all Indigenous led, and she hopes young people will see themselves as creators.

“Something that’s always been really important to me as a creative is being able to be a form of representation to young people out there, to young Indigenous youth specifically,” she said.

Murray said she also wants to lead by example and show you don’t need a degree or diploma backing your skills before you start creating.

“When Jamie and I began working [together], most of my products came from the dollar store and they were some of the … best works of art that I have ever presented or created, and that have been the most well received,” she said.

The Wendigo Project is currently in production with a public exhibition expected in Yellowknife later this year. Wetrade-Stevenson and Murray said they will share more details once they are finalized.

“We’re super excited to bring it to the community to just share and have it be known to the world,” Wetrade-Stevenson said.
